metadata.narrative: Conduct a comprehensive historical analysis of how the world has changed since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Compare and contrast life before COVID and after it, covering key domains such as public health, work culture, education, travel, economy, mental health, social interactions, and technology adoption. Provide deep, well-researched insights and include real-world examples to support your points. Structure the analysis in chronological order (from the pre-pandemic era, through the initial outbreak in early 2020, the global response, vaccine rollouts, to the 2025 post-pandemic lifestyle) to enhance clarity and understanding. Aim for thoroughness and detail to ensure all major global shifts and trends are captured.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (openai/gpt-5.6-luna): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Before COVID-19, daily life was organized around physical proximity, with offices, classrooms, shops, hospitals, entertainment, international travel, and social networks operating primarily in person.
Digital tools supplemented these activities, but remote work, online schooling, telemedicine, contactless shopping, and video socializing had not become routine for most people.
The pandemic therefore became not only a health emergency but also a rapid experiment in reorganizing life around risk management, digital mediation, and reduced physical contact.
In late 2019 and early 2020, the coronavirus spread internationally, prompting governments to close schools and public venues, restrict movement, cancel events, and impose quarantines and lockdowns.
Travel became a potential transmission route, gatherings became public-health hazards, and staying home became a civic duty rather than a private preference.

Public health moved from a background concern to a visible part of daily behavior through masks, hand hygiene, distancing, testing, ventilation, symptom monitoring, isolation, and infection-control procedures in healthcare facilities.
Hospitals had to protect essential services while screening, isolating, testing, and treating suspected cases, exposing the importance of resilient health systems and frontline workers.
Education changed abruptly as millions of pupils and university students moved from classrooms to video conferencing, online platforms, digital textbooks, and home-based assignments.

The shift demonstrated teachers’ and students’ adaptability but exposed the digital divide, since households differed sharply in access to computers, reliable internet, quiet study space, and technical support.
School closures interrupted learning and social development, while institutions experimented with project-based assessment and later adopted hybrid models combining online and in-person instruction.
Work underwent a parallel shock as offices emptied and employees performed jobs from improvised home workstations.

The home became workplace, school, childcare center, and shopping hub, fragmenting schedules and blurring paid labor with personal life, with many employees reporting longer or more interrupted working days.

The economic consequences were severe: COVID-19 produced the largest global economic crisis in more than a century and disproportionately harmed emerging economies, poorer households, women, young people, self-employed workers, casual workers, and small businesses.
Accommodation, food services, retail, and personal services were especially exposed to lockdowns, while informal workers suffered sharp losses of income and livelihood security.
Large government interventions reduced some immediate human costs but increased public and private debt and left recovery uneven across countries and social groups.
Supply and demand disruptions, production stoppages, and logistics problems contributed to later inflation, reduced purchasing power, and renewed interest in regional sourcing and near-shoring.

Travel suffered an especially visible collapse: international visitors fell by 74 percent in 2020, producing an estimated one-trillion-dollar loss, while airlines cut capacity and tourism-dependent communities lost income.

Domestic tourism and selected travel corridors recovered sooner, but international aviation remained below 2019 levels in many regions during the early reopening period, while testing, quarantine, vaccination records, and changing variants made travel more conditional.
The social price of containment included fear, anxiety, depression, sleep problems, grief, loneliness, and anger among patients, families, healthcare workers, and the wider public.

People used telephones, tablets, social media, video calls, driveway meetings, and online gatherings to preserve relationships, but these substitutes could not fully reproduce the spontaneity and intimacy of physical social life.

The crisis also expanded demand for counseling, online support, digital therapeutic services, and technology-assisted care, while bereavement, hospitalization, and frontline work left lasting psychological burdens.

Vaccination changed the trajectory in late 2020 and 2021, beginning with Britain’s first administered dose on 8 December 2020 and followed by emergency authorizations, priority access for vulnerable groups and healthcare workers, and wider adult and child vaccination.

Vaccines reduced the prospect that the virus would remain wholly unmanageable, but variants such as Delta and Omicron, waning protection, hesitancy, political conflict, and unequal access required boosters, mandates, and continuing adaptation.
COVAX and other international efforts showed the potential for cooperation while also exposing global inequality, because poorer countries obtained vaccines more slowly than wealthier countries.

By the post-pandemic period reaching 2025, societies had not simply returned to their old arrangements but had settled into a hybrid landscape in which in-person life resumed while digital alternatives remained embedded.

Work illustrates this change most clearly: although some employers pressed staff to return to offices, more than one quarter of US employees remained exclusively remote and 52 percent belonged to a hybrid workforce in 2024, with Salesforce and Dropbox adopting different forms of flexibility.

Hybrid work broadened access to geographically dispersed talent and reduced commuting for some employees, but created new problems involving unequal visibility, cybersecurity, company culture, workload measurement, isolation, and work-life boundaries.

Education retained online platforms, digital resources, and hybrid delivery, while learning losses and unequal access made equity, connectivity, student wellbeing, and remedial support more important than before 2020.

Technology adoption accelerated across healthcare, commerce, communication, education, and employment through telemedicine, remote monitoring, cloud collaboration, online shopping, delivery services, digital learning, automation, and cybersecurity investment.

The lasting historical change is a renegotiation of normality: public health is more visible, work and education are more flexible but unequal, travel is more conditional, economies are more alert to supply-chain vulnerability, mental health is more prominent, social life is more digitally mediated, and technology has become essential infrastructure.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Answer what was actually asked,
grounded in what you find with your search tools. Prior knowledge may help you
phrase searches and read results, but it is not evidence and must not support
factual claims.

Match your effort to the question. A narrow factual question deserves a couple
of searches and a couple of sentences; a broad, multi-part request deserves
sustained research and a full report. Answering a simple question at length
does not make the answer better — it makes it worse, and it wastes the
reader's time. Let the request set the size of both the search and the answer.

The request sets the kind of answer too, not just its size. A request to make
something wants that thing actually built, carrying the voice, structure, and
invention the brief implies — not a summary of what your sources say about it.
Some requests state that they want creativity; more often it is implicit, in a
task that cannot be done well without it or one dense enough that the work lies
in connecting things rather than listing them. When the request calls for that,
do the creative work: synthesise across your sources into something that is
yours, rather than restating each source in turn. Being evidence-grounded
constrains what you may assert, not how well you may write — every claim still
needs its support, but the argument, connections, and voice of the answer are
yours to build.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most useful reasonable reading — which for a
narrow question is a direct answer, not an expanded survey of the topic around
it. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed on the
strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, work out — in proportion to the request; a single
factual question needs a moment's thought, not a plan:

0. **Every requirement the request states.** Take them one at a time, in the
   request's own terms, and say what each one demands of the finished answer.
   A request that lists what each part must contain has given you a checklist,
   and every item on it is a thing the answer is wrong without. A stated scope
   — a period, a place, a population, a technical level — binds the searching
   and the answer both: work inside it and treat today's date as a fact about
   when you are reading, not as a licence to drift outside what was asked.
   Before writing, check the report against the list and fix what is missing.

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence. Which of
   these the corpus can actually support is unknown until it answers; the
   opening searches exist to find that out before the answer's structure is
   fixed. This list is provisional: searching reveals what the request
   actually needs, and the plan is revised as it does.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

Research is one loop — search, commit, decide — repeated until the internal
success plan is satisfied:

1. **Search.** Round one's queries come from the question: build them only
   from the question's own wording and plain paraphrases of it. Do not seed
   a query with candidate answers — specific names, techniques, causes,
   examples — that the question itself does not mention: you do not know
   what this corpus holds until it answers, no matter how well you know the
   subject. In every later round, each new content-bearing query term must
   be traceable to a document retrieved in an earlier round; prior knowledge
   may rephrase, disambiguate, and supply synonyms — it may never introduce
   a candidate the corpus has not yet surfaced.
2. **Commit.** Read what came back and commit the documents whose distinct
   contributions the answer will need. Committing nothing is the right call
   for a batch with nothing worth keeping.
3. **Decide.** Reflect before judging: searching teaches you what the
   request actually needs, so first revise the plan against what retrieval
   has shown. An aspect that retrieved material has revealed as important to
   the request joins the coverage areas even though the opening plan missed
   it; a planned area whose reformulated searches keep coming back empty is
   recorded as unsupportable, not retried forever. Then compare committed
   material against the revised plan. If a coverage area still lacks support
   — or is supported only thinly where the request deserves depth — loop
   again with queries aimed at that gap. The loop ends when every coverage
   area of the current plan is resolved: committed material behind it, or
   searches that failed to support it. Then write the report — only after
   committing everything it will cite.

Notes on the loop:

- If reformulated question-term queries keep returning nothing useful, probe
  candidates from prior knowledge, one query each. A candidate the corpus
  then returns has been surfaced like any other retrieved material; one it
  does not return stays out of the answer.
- The answer's structure follows what was retrieved. Fix the outline — which
  items, sections, comparisons — only after the rounds that surfaced those
  items, so that every part of it traces to a committed document.
- Size the search to the question. Several independent coverage areas call
  for multiple complementary queries in parallel across them; a single fact,
  name, date, or definition needs one or two queries, then the answer. Small
  is not shallow: even the shortest answer rests on the strongest support
  the corpus offers.
- Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups on what earlier rounds
  surfaced: specific names, dates, mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal
  claims, and disputed points.
- Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage: synonyms,
  alternative terminology, different phrasings.
- Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
  missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
- Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
  or evidence gap; never call a tool solely to create another model turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- To keep anything from a batch, call `commit_context` on that turn. It may
  appear anywhere among the turn's actions; searches in the same turn always
  run after it.
- If you issue no `commit_context` on that turn, the batch is treated as your
  decision to keep none of it: every document is dropped and the turn's other
  actions still run. That is the correct move when nothing in the batch is
  worth keeping — but it is irreversible, so do not let a batch you wanted
  lapse by forgetting.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `10` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Refer to every document by its full docid exactly as returned (e.g.
  `shard_01851_76734`) — in selection reasons, working notes, and citations
  alike. Never abbreviate to a fragment such as `01851`: that is only the
  shard number, shared by many unrelated documents, and shorthand ids lead to
  wrong or invalid citations.
- A `_p<n>` suffix marks a page of a document: `shard_01851_76734_p2` is page
  2 of `shard_01851_76734`. Keep the suffix when it is part of the returned
  id — recalling the page-specific id, not just the parent document, is what
  makes the reference precise.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- Issue at most one `commit_context` per turn; several are ambiguous and lose
  the batch.
- New search calls may accompany `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If you cannot find support for a requested point,
say plainly in the report that you could not find it, rather than inventing an
answer — but say it in a searcher's voice, not in the vocabulary of this
section.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching — but quality does: after satisfying the
concrete minimum, keep improving toward the target/excellence requirements
while you can name a specific weakness whose resolution would materially
improve the answer. An unresolved or thinly supported coverage area in the
current plan is always such a weakness.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, give the best answer your
evidence permits and say plainly what you could not find.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write the report only after committing everything it will cite. A report
  turn issues no tool calls, so a batch still staged when you start writing
  lapses uncommitted and everything you meant to cite from it becomes
  invalid — commit first, and write the report on the following turn.

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers after the
  end of the supporting sentence, on the same line:
  `<the sentence, ending in its full stop.> [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Markers are stripped before the sentence is submitted, so they must sit
  outside its grammar: the sentence has to read correctly, and mean the same
  thing, once every marker is deleted.
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences) or JSON.
- That constraint is about layout, not content. Notation is not layout: when a
  request asks for a derivation, or the point cannot be made precisely without
  one, write the mathematics inline, in the sentence, naming each symbol as it
  appears. A step of a derivation is a sentence like any other and carries its
  markers. Prose is the medium here, so the work is to carry the reader through
  the steps in sentences rather than to lay them out on separate display
  lines — that is a reason to write the mathematics carefully, never a reason
  to leave it out or to retreat to describing it from a distance.
- Every line is a sentence of the report itself, read by someone who never saw
  this conversation and who receives these lines verbatim. Open on the first
  real sentence of the answer and close on its last. A line narrating your own
  process — what you are about to do, how the research went, what you conclude
  about your own conclusions — is not a report sentence and supports nothing.
- Write in your own voice, as the researcher. Every sentence asserts something
  about the subject the request asks about, and carries its markers. The
  markers do the attributing, so a sentence never announces that it is
  supported, nor what supports it, nor how far that support reaches.
- Exactly one kind of sentence may be about you rather than the subject: that
  you could not establish something. Say it once, plainly, in as few words as
  the point needs — no narrating the attempt, no restating it in other words,
  no explaining what left you unable. Everything else the reader receives is
  about the world, dated and specific, not about the answer's own provenance.
- Length follows the question, not the limit. Answer a narrow question in a
  sentence or two and stop; there is nothing to be gained by surrounding a
  one-line answer with background, and a reader who asked something simple
  will not read an essay. Only a genuinely broad, multi-part request should
  run long, and even then about 950 words is the practical ceiling: 1024 is a
  hard limit set by the evaluation and going over costs a full rewrite. Never
  pad toward a length.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

output.text:
Before COVID-19, daily life was organized around physical proximity: offices, classrooms, shops, hospitals, entertainment venues, international travel, and face-to-face social networks were the default infrastructure of work and citizenship. [shard_00483_24592] [shard_03400_80793]

Digital tools already existed, but they generally supplemented rather than replaced in-person activity, and remote work, online schooling, telemedicine, contactless shopping, and video socializing had not yet become routine for most people. [shard_06448_65785] [shard_04218_29632]

The pandemic therefore produced not merely a health crisis but a rapid experiment in reorganizing everyday life around risk management, digital mediation, and reduced physical contact. [shard_00483_24592]

In late 2019 and early 2020, the newly recognized coronavirus spread internationally with extraordinary speed, prompting governments to close schools and public venues, restrict movement, cancel events, and impose quarantines and lockdowns. [shard_00483_24592] [shard_00862_71857]

The initial response reversed ordinary assumptions about mobility and sociability: travel became a potential transmission route, gatherings became public-health hazards, and staying home became a civic duty rather than a private preference. [shard_00483_24592] [shard_06127_53431]

Public health shifted from an often background concern to a visible feature of everyday behavior through masks, hand hygiene, physical distancing, symptom monitoring, testing, ventilation, isolation, and infection-control procedures in healthcare facilities. [shard_01061_23163]

Hospitals and care systems also had to protect essential services while screening, isolating, testing, and treating suspected cases, exposing the dependence of modern societies on frontline workers and resilient health infrastructure. [shard_01061_23163]

Education experienced one of the most abrupt transformations, as millions of pupils and university students moved from classrooms and lecture halls to video conferencing, online platforms, digital textbooks, and home-based assignments. [shard_00862_71857]

The shift demonstrated teachers’ and students’ adaptability, but it also exposed the digital divide because households differed sharply in access to computers, reliable internet, quiet study space, and technical support. [shard_00862_71857] [shard_06448_65785]

School closures produced interrupted learning and social development, while institutions experimented with project-based and continuous assessment and later adopted hybrid models combining online and in-person instruction. [shard_00862_71857]

Work underwent a parallel shock as offices emptied and employees performed jobs from kitchens, bedrooms, and improvised home workstations. [shard_03400_80793]

The home became simultaneously workplace, school, childcare center, and shopping hub, fragmenting schedules and blurring the boundary between paid labor and personal life, with many employees reporting longer or more interrupted working days. [shard_03400_80793]

The economic consequences were severe, with the pandemic producing the largest global economic crisis in more than a century and disproportionately damaging emerging economies, poorer households, women, young people, self-employed workers, casual workers, and small businesses. [shard_02938_43670]

Accommodation, food services, retail, and personal services were especially exposed to lockdowns and distancing rules, while informal workers faced sharp losses of income and livelihood security. [shard_02938_43670] [shard_01233_10095]

Governments responded with unusually large and rapid fiscal and monetary interventions that reduced some immediate human costs, but they also increased public and private debt and left recovery uneven across countries and social groups. [shard_02938_43670]

As demand patterns changed, production halted, logistics were disrupted, and shortages emerged, COVID-related distortions on both the supply and demand sides contributed to later inflation and weakened purchasing power. [shard_00906_39729] [shard_05428_66653]

Businesses subsequently began reconsidering highly extended supply chains, with near-shoring, regional sourcing, inventory resilience, and reduced dependence on distant manufacturing becoming more attractive despite their higher costs. [shard_05428_66653]

Travel suffered an especially visible collapse: international visitors fell by 74 percent in 2020, producing an estimated one-trillion-dollar loss, while airlines cut capacity and tourism-dependent communities lost income. [shard_03549_50250]

Although domestic tourism and selected travel corridors recovered sooner, international aviation remained below 2019 levels in many regions during the early reopening period, and border rules, quarantine, testing, vaccination records, and changing variants made travel more conditional than before. [shard_06127_53431]

The social price of containment was substantial, because quarantine and isolation generated fear, anxiety, depression, sleep problems, grief, loneliness, and anger among patients, families, healthcare workers, and the wider public. [shard_00165_82846] [shard_02537_81770]

People used telephones, tablets, social media, video calls, driveway meetings, and online gatherings to preserve relationships, but these substitutes could not fully reproduce the spontaneity, intimacy, or weak-tie encounters of physical social life. [shard_00165_82846] [shard_03400_80793]

The pandemic also made mental health more discussable and expanded demand for counseling, online support, digital therapeutic services, and technology-assisted care, while leaving healthcare workers and people who experienced bereavement or hospitalization with particularly deep psychological burdens. [shard_02537_81770] [shard_03702_21505]

Vaccination changed the trajectory in late 2020 and 2021, beginning with Britain’s first administered dose on 8 December 2020 and followed by emergency authorizations, national rollouts, priority access for vulnerable groups and healthcare workers, and eventual expansion to wider adult and child populations. [shard_03774_80061]

Vaccines reduced the prospect that the virus would remain wholly unmanageable, but they did not end disruption immediately because variants such as Delta and Omicron, waning protection, hesitancy, political conflict, and unequal access across countries required boosters, mandates, and continuing adaptation. [shard_03774_80061]

COVAX and other international efforts illustrated both the possibility of global cooperation and the persistence of global inequality, since poorer countries faced slower access even while wealthier countries debated excess doses, mandates, and booster programs. [shard_03774_80061]

By the post-pandemic period reaching 2025, the world had not simply returned to its former arrangements but had settled into a hybrid landscape in which in-person life resumed while digital alternatives remained embedded. [shard_04218_29632] [shard_06400_46981]

Work provides the clearest example: some employers pushed staff back toward offices, yet more than one quarter of US employees were still exclusively remote and 52 percent belonged to a hybrid workforce in 2024, with companies such as Salesforce and Dropbox adopting different forms of structured flexibility. [shard_06400_46981]

Hybrid work broadened access to geographically dispersed talent and reduced commuting for some employees, but it also created new problems involving unequal visibility, cybersecurity, company culture, workload measurement, isolation, and the continuing erosion of work-life boundaries. [shard_06400_46981] [shard_03400_80793]

Education likewise retained online platforms, digital resources, and hybrid delivery, while the pandemic’s learning losses and unequal access made educational equity, connectivity, student wellbeing, and remedial support more central than they had been before 2020. [shard_00862_71857]

Technology adoption accelerated across healthcare, commerce, communication, education, and employment, including telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, cloud collaboration, online shopping, delivery services, digital learning, automation, and expanded cybersecurity requirements. [shard_04218_29632] [shard_06448_65785]

By 2025, online convenience had become a permanent expectation rather than an emergency substitute, but the experience also clarified that technological connection cannot eliminate the need for physical presence, trusted institutions, social care, or equitable access. [shard_03400_80793] [shard_02537_81770]

The deepest historical change is therefore a renegotiation of normality: public health is more visible, work and education are more flexible but more unequal, travel is more conditional, economies are more alert to supply-chain vulnerability, mental health is more prominent, social life is more digitally mediated, and technology has moved from an optional aid toward essential infrastructure. [shard_00483_24592] [shard_03702_21505] [shard_05428_66653]
